passage:
Monday: At the school fair, Sarita sat cross-legged in front of the puppet show, mouth open as the tiger puppet chased the monkey. Her Masi, Himani, walked right past the front row with a tray of lemonade. Sarita didn't blink.
Tuesday: "I waved at you!" said Himani Masi. "No, you didn't come," said Sarita, very sure.
Saturday: At the next show, Masi sat beside Sarita and whispered, "Watch the puppets, but look for me when they bow." When the puppets bowed, Sarita turned and squealed. "You're here!"

qa.q: What was Himani Masi carrying when she walked past?
qa.a: She was carrying a tray of lemonade.

qa.q: Why was Sarita so sure Himani Masi hadn't come?
qa.a: Sarita was so absorbed and delighted by the tiger chasing the monkey that Masi simply didn't register, so she felt truly confident that Masi had not come.

qa.q: What small trick helped on Saturday?
qa.a: Masi sat close and gave a clear moment to look, when the puppets bowed, so Sarita could enjoy the show and still notice her.

qa.q: How might Himani Masi have felt when Sarita said she didn't come?
qa.a: She may have felt a little hurt or puzzled, having walked right past, until she realised Sarita was just deep in the show.

grounding: It shows a preschooler watching a puppet show who misses her aunt walking right past, because attention pulls to one focus.

The temple fair was loud: drums, bells, a balloon seller shouting. Santosh, five, sat on the mat in front of the puppet stage while his mother, Hansa, searched the nearby steps for his lost sandal, glancing back at him every few seconds.
She found it and walked past the stage waving it, calling his name. His eyes stayed on the king puppet's golden crown. She passed again with a water bottle, right in front of him. Nothing.
When the show ended he turned and saw her. "Amma, you went away!"
"Kanna, I walked past you twice!"
He shook his head, very sure. "No. Only the king was there."

qa.q: What were Santosh's eyes fixed on?
qa.a: His eyes stayed on the king puppet's golden crown.

qa.q: Why was Santosh so sure his mother had gone away?
qa.a: Santosh was so absorbed in the king puppet's golden crown that his mother vanished for him, so he truly felt she had gone away and was upset about it.

qa.q: What could Hansa do at the next busy show?
qa.a: Sit beside him or touch his shoulder when she comes back, instead of expecting him to notice her walking by in the noise.

qa.q: What is it like for Hansa when Santosh says she went away?
qa.a: She is probably surprised and a little amused 😅, since she walked right past him twice while keeping an eye on him.

grounding: It shows a preschooler at a noisy fair who misses his mother walking past twice because his attention is fixed on the puppet show.

passage:
In the colony hall in Chennai, the Sunday puppet show had begun. Sonali, five, sat in the front row as the crow puppet tried to steal the grandmother's vadai.
Behind the rows, her father, Saurabh, walked slowly across the hall carrying a huge red balloon he had bought for her. He even stopped and bounced it near the front. Other children pointed. Sonali didn't turn.
After the show he held out the balloon. "Did you see me walk past?"
Sonali's eyes went wide. "When? You weren't here!"
"I was right there, with this big red thing."
She stared at the balloon as if it had appeared by magic.

qa.q: What was Saurabh carrying across the hall?
qa.a: He was carrying a huge red balloon he had bought for Sonali.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stare at the balloon as if it had appeared by magic?
qa.a: Sonali was surprised and amazed, because her attention had been so fixed on the crow and the vadai that she never saw the balloon until it appeared in front of her.

qa.q: What could Saurabh learn about getting Sonali's attention?
qa.a: When she is deep in something, even a big red balloon may not register; going close and speaking to her directly works better.

qa.q: Why might the other children have noticed Saurabh when Sonali didn't?
qa.a: They weren't as locked onto the puppets at that moment, so the balloon caught their eye, while Sonali's attention had no room left for it.

grounding: It shows a preschooler absorbed in a puppet show who misses her father walking past with a balloon, as attention pulls to one focus.

"Darshan, did you like the puppet show?"
"Yes, Dadu! The king puppet fell off the horse, and the horse danced!"
"Did you see Mama walk right past you in the middle of it? She was carrying the ice cream."
"No! Mama didn't come."
"She did. She walked in front of the stage and waved."
Darshan frowned. "I was watching the king. I didn't see anything else."
Dadu laughed. "That's how eyes work, little one. When you look hard at one thing, the rest goes away."
"Where's my ice cream, then?"
"Melting, in Mama's hand. Run!"

qa.q: What happened to the king puppet?
qa.a: The king puppet fell off the horse.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel about the puppet show and about missing Mama?
qa.a: Darshan felt excited by the king puppet and the dancing horse, and then surprised and puzzled to hear Mama had walked right past, frowning because nothing else had been noticed.

qa.q: How did Dadu handle Darshan's surprise, and why was that helpful?
qa.a: He laughed kindly and explained that looking hard at one thing makes the rest go away, so Darshan learned it was normal, not a silly mistake.

qa.q: What might Mama have felt when she waved and got no response?
qa.a: She may have been amused, seeing how completely the show had caught Darshan's attention even as she walked in front of the stage.

grounding: A preschooler watching a puppet show misses Mama walking right past, because attention locks onto one focus.

passage:
Teacher's note, KG-A, Friday. Payal
A puppet group visited today. During the story of the clever crow, our principal slowly crossed the back of the hall carrying a tall plant in a red pot. Afterwards I asked Indu, who sat in front, "Did anyone walk past during the show?" Indu said firmly, "No, Ma'am. Only the crow." When I told the class about the principal, Indu's eyes went round. "A PLANT? I didn't see!"
What I did next: we talked about how our eyes follow whatever our mind is busy with. Everyone giggled 😊

qa.q: What was the principal carrying across the hall?
qa.a: A tall plant in a red pot.

qa.q: What do Indu's round eyes suggest when hearing about the principal?
qa.a: They suggest real surprise; Indu had been so wrapped up in the crow that the principal simply wasn't seen.

qa.q: How did Payal turn the surprise into something useful for the class?
qa.a: She talked with them about how eyes follow whatever the mind is busy with, so missing the plant felt interesting rather than embarrassing.

qa.q: What might the principal have thought, walking across and seeing no heads turn?
qa.a: The principal may have been amused, seeing how completely the puppets held the children's attention.

grounding: A teacher notes a preschooler so absorbed in a puppet show that a person crossing the hall with a plant goes unseen.

passage:
Nursery class note, Friday.
We had a puppet show today: a crow and a fox arguing over a piece of cheese. Siddharth sat in the front row, mouth open. Halfway through, Vidya ma'am from the office walked right across the back of the stage carrying a tall stack of chairs and wearing a bright orange dupatta. Almost every child turned. Siddharth didn't blink. Afterwards, when the others giggled about the orange chair lady, Siddharth frowned. "What lady?" He insisted there had been no lady. I told him it's normal: when we watch one thing very hard, other things can disappear. He thought that was like magic.

qa.q: What were the crow and the fox arguing over?
qa.a: A piece of cheese.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth insist there had been no lady?
qa.a: Siddharth felt sure and puzzled, because he had been so absorbed in the puppets that Vidya ma'am never entered his attention.

qa.q: How did the teacher explain it, and why is that a helpful way to put it?
qa.a: The teacher said watching one thing hard can make other things disappear, which helps Siddharth see it as normal, not a mistake.

qa.q: How might the other children see Siddharth's 'What lady?'
qa.a: They might find it funny or surprising, since the orange dupatta and chairs seemed impossible to miss.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so fixed on a puppet show that he misses a person walking across the stage.

passage: At the village fair in Nagaur, the kathputli puppets danced on their strings while the drum beat fast. Raghav, five, sat on the dusty ground, eyes fixed on the puppet king waving his sword. His big sister Arohi, back from buying balloons, walked right in front of him holding three red ones, and even waved. Raghav didn't move. When the show ended, he jumped up. "Where's Arohi didi? She's been gone so long!" Arohi laughed and held out a balloon. "I walked past you! I waved!" Raghav's mouth fell open. "You did not." "I did." He looked at the empty stage, then back at her, and wondered how.

qa.q: What colour were the balloons Arohi carried?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why did Raghav think Arohi had been gone so long?
qa.a: Raghav felt surprised and a little worried, because he was so absorbed in the puppet king that he never saw her walk past and wave.

qa.q: What could help Raghav understand what happened?
qa.a: A grown-up could explain gently that when we watch one thing very closely, other things can pass unseen.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when Raghav said 'You did not'?
qa.a: Arohi was amused and laughed, knowing she had walked right in front of him.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so absorbed in a puppet show that he misses his sister walking past and waving.

passage: At the library in Oslo, Ulla, five, sat cross-legged in front of the puppet theatre, watching a clumsy troll try to bake a cake. She laughed so hard she hiccupped. While the troll dropped the eggs, a librarian in a big yellow raincoat pushed a squeaky book trolley right behind the theatre. Ulla's friend Nkechi pointed and whispered. Ulla didn't turn her head. After the show, Nkechi said, "Did you see the trolley? It squeaked so loud!" Ulla blinked. "What trolley?" She was sure there hadn't been one. They asked the librarian, who laughed and pointed at the trolley by the door.

qa.q: What was the troll trying to do?
qa.a: The troll was trying to bake a cake.

qa.q: Why was Ulla so sure there hadn't been a trolley?
qa.a: Ulla felt certain and surprised, because she was so absorbed in the troll that the squeaky trolley never reached her attention.

qa.q: What might a grown-up tell Ulla about this?
qa.a: That when we focus hard on one thing, our attention hides the rest, which is normal and even a bit funny.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Ulla said 'What trolley?'
qa.a: Nkechi might have felt puzzled and amused, since the trolley seemed so loud and obvious.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so fixed on a puppet show that a noisy trolley passing behind goes unnoticed.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when the children said they didn't see him?

It was a cold winter morning and the school's puppet show had been moved into the small hall because of fog. Nitin, five, squeezed between other children on the mat. The hall was crowded and noisy, and he had to lean to see.

A puppet crocodile snapped at a puppet monkey. Nitin gasped.

While he watched, his teacher Zubin sir walked past with a big box of blankets. Nitin didn't look up.

Afterwards Zubin sir asked, "Did anyone see me carry blankets?"

"No!" Nitin said. "You were here?"

"I walked right past you."

Nitin's mouth fell open. "But I was watching the crocodile!"

qa.q: What was Zubin sir carrying?
qa.a: A big box of blankets.

qa.q: What does Nitin's mouth falling open suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shocked and amazed that he missed his teacher walking right past him.

qa.q: How could Zubin sir help the children understand what happened?
qa.a: He could explain that watching one exciting thing can make us miss other things, even big ones.

qa.q: What is it like for Zubin sir when nobody noticed him?
qa.a: He might feel amused, knowing children's attention was fully on the crocodile.

At the Dussehra fair in the Jaipur colony, a puppet show was on: a wooden king and a clever parrot, arguing in squeaky voices.
Deepak, five, sat in the front row, mouth open. His cousin Ankita Didi walked right past the stage twice, waving a big pink balloon at him.
After the show she asked, "Did you see me with the balloon?"
"No! When?"
"Twice! Right in front!"
Deepak shook his head, amazed. He had only seen the parrot. "The parrot was so funny," he said. Then, "Can I have the balloon now?"

qa.q: What colour was Ankita Didi's balloon?
qa.a: The balloon was big and pink.

qa.q: Why didn't Deepak see Ankita Didi walk past?
qa.a: Deepak was delighted and absorbed in the parrot, so his attention held only the puppet show.

qa.q: What could Ankita Didi do next time she wants Deepak to notice her during a show?
qa.a: Ankita Didi could wait until the show ends, or sit beside him, since his attention is fixed on the puppets.

qa.q: How did Ankita Didi feel when Deepak said 'No! When?'
qa.a: Ankita Didi was surprised and amused that he hadn't seen her twice, right in front.

grounding: Shows a preschooler at a puppet show whose attention is so fixed on the parrot that a cousin walking past vanishes.

passage:
Summer camp note, May. Written by Kunal, activity teacher.
At Thursday's clown show, Darshan sat at the front, eyes fixed on the clown's red nose. Halfway through, a dog wandered across the stage. Every other child pointed.
After the show I asked Darshan, "Did you see the dog?" He looked shocked. "What dog?"
He wasn't being silly. His attention was completely on the red nose.
What I did next: I told his parents this is normal at his age, and that touching his shoulder and waiting for his eyes helps.

qa.q: What was Darshan staring at during the clown show?
qa.a: Darshan's eyes were fixed on the clown's red nose.

qa.q: Why didn't Darshan see the dog?
qa.a: Darshan was delighted and focused on the red nose, so his attention held nothing else.

qa.q: What did Kunal suggest to Darshan's parents, and why?
qa.a: To touch his shoulder and wait for his eyes before speaking, since his attention locks onto one thing.

qa.q: How did the other children experience the dog?
qa.a: The other children noticed it and pointed, excited by the surprise.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a preschooler so fixed on a clown's nose that a dog crossing the stage goes unseen.

qa.a: A basket of oranges.

qa.q: How could a grown-up get Simran's attention during a show?
